prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

The equilibration of macroscopic degrees of freedom during the fusion of heavy nuclei, like the charge and the shape, are studied in the Time-Dependent Hartree-Fock theory. The pre-equilibrium Giant Dipole Resonance (GDR) is used to probe the fusion path. It is shown that such isovector collective state is excited in N/Z asymmetric fusion and to a less extent in mass asymmetric systems. The characteristics of this GDR are governed by the structure of the fused system in its preequilibrium phase, like its deformation, rotation and vibration. In particular, we show that a lowering of the pre-equilibrium GDR energy is expected as compared to the statistical one. Revisiting experimental data, we extract an evidence of this lowering for the first time. We also quantify the fusion-evaporation enhancement due to gamma-ray emission from the pre-equilibrium GDR. This cooling mechanism along the fusion path may be suitable to synthesize in the future super heavy elements using radioactive beams with strong N/Z asymmetries in the entrance channel.

outputs.L1: The equilibration of macroscopic degrees of freedom, such as charge and shape, during the fusion of heavy nuclei is studied within the Time-Dependent Hartree–Fock framework. The pre-equilibrium Giant Dipole Resonance (GDR) is used to probe the fusion pathway. We show that this isovector collective state is excited in fusion reactions with N/Z asymmetry and, to a lesser extent, in mass-asymmetric systems. The characteristics of the GDR are governed by the structure of the fused system during its pre-equilibrium phase, including its deformation, rotation, and vibration. In particular, we demonstrate that the pre-equilibrium GDR energy is expected to be lower than its statistical counterpart. By revisiting experimental data, we identify evidence of this energy reduction for the first time. We also quantify the enhancement of fusion–evaporation arising from gamma-ray emission by the pre-equilibrium GDR. This cooling mechanism along the fusion pathway may facilitate the future synthesis of superheavy elements using radioactive beams with strong N/Z asymmetries in the entrance channel.
outputs.L2: Time-Dependent Hartree-Fock theory is employed to investigate how macroscopic variables, including charge and shape, equilibrate during heavy-nucleus fusion. The fusion trajectory is examined through the pre-equilibrium Giant Dipole Resonance (GDR). This isovector collective mode is strongly excited when the colliding nuclei have different neutron-to-proton ratios and, more weakly, when their masses are unequal. Its properties reflect the configuration of the newly fused system before equilibrium is reached, particularly its deformation, rotational motion, and vibrations. The analysis predicts that the pre-equilibrium GDR should have a lower energy than the corresponding statistical GDR. A reanalysis of experimental results provides the first evidence for this energy reduction. The increase in fusion-evaporation probability caused by gamma-ray emission from the pre-equilibrium GDR is also quantified. By cooling the system during fusion, this process could eventually help produce superheavy elements with radioactive beams that create large entrance-channel N/Z asymmetries.
outputs.L3:
Time-Dependent Hartree-Fock (TDHF) theory provides a microscopic framework for investigating the equilibration of macroscopic properties during the fusion of heavy nuclei. In particular, it can describe how quantities such as charge distribution and nuclear shape evolve as the colliding nuclei merge and form a highly excited composite system.

An important signature of this early fusion dynamics is the pre-equilibrium Giant Dipole Resonance (GDR), a collective oscillation of protons against neutrons that develops before the fused system reaches statistical equilibrium. This mode acts as a probe of the fusion pathway because its excitation depends strongly on the properties of the entrance channel. It is especially pronounced when the colliding nuclei have substantially different neutron-to-proton ratios, or \(N/Z\) values. By contrast, mass-asymmetric reactions generally produce a weaker pre-equilibrium dipole excitation.

The properties of the pre-equilibrium GDR are determined by the evolving structure and motion of the newly formed system. Its energy, strength, and time dependence are influenced by the deformation of the composite nucleus, its rotation, and its collective vibrations. TDHF calculations predict that the energy of this early dipole mode should be lower than that of the statistical GDR emitted after equilibration. Reanalyses of experimental gamma-ray data have provided the first evidence for this predicted energy reduction.

Gamma-ray emission from the pre-equilibrium GDR may also affect the outcome of the reaction. By removing energy from the composite system at an early stage, it provides an additional cooling mechanism that can enhance the probability of fusion followed by evaporation rather than fission. This effect could be particularly valuable in attempts to synthesize superheavy elements using radioactive nuclear beams, where large entrance-channel \(N/Z\) asymmetries may generate strong pre-equilibrium dipole oscillations and thereby improve the survival probability of the fused nucleus.
outputs.L4:
Heavy-ion fusion involves a rapid and complex reorganization of nuclear matter. When two nuclei come into contact, their initially different neutron-to-proton ratios, densities, and shapes begin to equilibrate. These early processes can strongly influence whether the collision produces a compound nucleus or instead ends in reseparation through quasi-fission or another non-fusion channel. They are particularly important for reactions involving nuclei with markedly different masses or neutron-to-proton ratios, as may occur when neutron-rich radioactive beams are used to synthesize very heavy and superheavy elements.

Time-Dependent Hartree-Fock theory provides a microscopic framework for investigating this nonequilibrium stage. In TDHF, protons and neutrons evolve self-consistently in the mean field generated by all the nucleons. The method therefore describes, within a single dynamical calculation, changes in density, deformation, nucleon transfer, and collective motion. By following the proton and neutron distributions in time, one can examine how quickly charge equilibration occurs and how it is coupled to the evolving shape of the composite system.

A prominent signature of this dynamics is the pre-equilibrium Giant Dipole Resonance. If the projectile and target have different neutron-to-proton ratios, the newly formed system initially contains an uneven distribution of isospin. This imbalance can generate an oscillation in which the neutron and proton fluids move against one another. The resulting collective mode resembles the ordinary Giant Dipole Resonance of an equilibrated nucleus, but it develops before the compound system has reached thermal and shape equilibrium. Its properties consequently retain information about the entrance channel and the early fusion dynamics.

TDHF calculations can be used to track the associated dipole moment and its time dependence. The calculations show that charge equilibration is not necessarily a simple, monotonic redistribution of neutrons and protons. Instead, it may proceed through damped collective oscillations whose frequency and lifetime depend on the mass asymmetry, the initial neutron-to-proton imbalance, the collision geometry, and the deformation of the evolving system. Shape equilibration takes place on a related timescale: the elongated configuration produced when the nuclei first merge gradually evolves toward a more compact compound-nuclear shape.

Because the pre-equilibrium system is generally more elongated than an equilibrated nucleus, its dipole restoring force is weaker along the long axis. The pre-equilibrium GDR is therefore expected to emit gamma rays with lower characteristic energies than the statistical GDR formed later in the hot compound nucleus. Experimental gamma-ray spectra support this interpretation, revealing an additional low-energy dipole component that cannot be explained solely by statistical decay. The observation provides evidence that collective proton-neutron motion occurs during the earliest stage of fusion.

This prompt dipole radiation also affects the subsequent survival of the compound nucleus. Gamma-ray emission removes excitation energy without changing the nuclear mass or charge. By cooling the system before statistical particle evaporation and fission fully develop, the pre-equilibrium GDR can reduce the probability of fission and increase the likelihood that the compound nucleus survives through an evaporation-residue channel. In this sense, the mode is not merely a diagnostic of charge equilibration; it can influence the final reaction outcome.

The effect may be especially valuable in attempts to produce superheavy elements. Such nuclei are formed with very small cross sections and face intense competition between neutron evaporation and fission. Reactions using neutron-rich radioactive beams could provide favorable neutron-to-proton asymmetries and excite stronger prompt dipole oscillations. If the resulting gamma-ray cooling increases compound-nucleus survival, carefully chosen asymmetric entrance channels may offer an additional means of improving superheavy-element production. Thus, the combined theoretical and experimental study of the pre-equilibrium GDR connects microscopic charge and shape equilibration with the practical search for new nuclei at the limits of stability.
outputs.L5:
### The Time-Dependent World

The world is shaped by time. Seasons change, cities grow, memories fade, and people become different versions of themselves. Nothing remains entirely fixed; every life, relationship, and decision is time-dependent.

What seems impossible today may become ordinary tomorrow. A painful experience can slowly turn into wisdom, while a brief opportunity can disappear if it is ignored. Time does not merely measure events—it changes their meaning.

Recognizing that life is time-dependent encourages us to value the present. We cannot control every change, but we can choose how we respond to it. The passing of time is not only a reminder of what we lose; it is also the source of growth, renewal, and possibility.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an abstract for a nuclear physics paper on pre-equilibrium giant dipole resonances in heavy-ion fusion studied with Time-Dependent Hartree-Fock theory.
counterfactuals.output: We investigate pre-equilibrium giant dipole resonances generated during charge-asymmetric heavy-ion fusion using three-dimensional Time-Dependent Hartree-Fock theory. The collective isovector response is characterized through the time evolution of the proton–neutron dipole moment and its conjugate momentum, while the associated prompt γ-ray spectrum is obtained from the Fourier transform of the dipole acceleration. The calculations follow the system from the entrance channel through neck formation and the development of a compact composite configuration, providing a microscopic description of the coupling between dipole oscillations, deformation, and fusion dynamics. We examine the dependence of the response on collision geometry, beam energy, and entrance-channel charge asymmetry. The pre-equilibrium mode is found to exhibit a strongly time-dependent frequency and damping, reflecting the evolving shape and density of the composite system. Its γ-ray emission is anisotropic and occurs before statistical equilibration, making it a sensitive probe of early-time isovector dynamics. These results demonstrate that TDHF offers a consistent framework for connecting entrance-channel properties with prompt dipole radiation and for constraining the nuclear symmetry energy under dynamical, sub-saturation conditions.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize research investigating how charge and shape equilibrate during asymmetric nuclear fusion, including GDR energy shifts, gamma-ray cooling, and implications for superheavy-element synthesis.
counterfactuals.output:
Research on asymmetric heavy-ion fusion examines how a projectile and target with different neutron-to-proton ratios evolve toward a single compound nucleus. Time-dependent mean-field calculations, transport models, and prompt γ-ray measurements give a broadly consistent picture:

- **Charge equilibration is rapid.** Neutrons and protons flow through the developing neck, damping the initial \(N/Z\) imbalance on a timescale of roughly \(10^{-22}\)–\(10^{-21}\) s. The associated proton–neutron oscillation is called the **dynamical dipole** or pre-equilibrium giant dipole resonance (GDR).
- **Shape equilibration is generally slower.** The initially elongated, necked dinuclear configuration must contract and redistribute mass and angular momentum. Thus charge can be nearly equilibrated while strong quadrupole deformation and entrance-channel memory remain. In very heavy systems, this slow shape evolution competes with quasifission.

The changing shape alters the GDR restoring force. An elongated system has a lower dipole frequency along its long axis, so early dynamical-dipole γ rays are often shifted to **lower energies** than the equilibrium GDR expected for a compact compound nucleus. Transverse modes may lie at higher energy, producing deformation-induced splitting. As the nucleus becomes more compact, the centroid moves toward the ordinary statistical-GDR energy; damping, rotation, temperature, and the finite fusion time broaden the observed spectrum.

Emission of these prompt γ rays removes excitation energy—and some angular momentum—before statistical neutron evaporation and fission dominate. The total energy removed is usually modest, but for nuclei near the fission threshold even a small amount of **pre-equilibrium γ cooling** can increase the probability that the fused system survives rather than undergoing fission. Models therefore suggest that charge-asymmetric entrance channels could aid superheavy-element synthesis by simultaneously promoting dynamical-dipole radiation and providing an experimental probe of whether a compact compound nucleus was reached.

The practical benefit remains conditional: γ-emission probabilities are limited, and capture, quasifission, shell effects, angular momentum, and neutron separation energies usually have larger effects on final evaporation-residue yields. Consequently, GDR energy shifts and prompt γ yields are best viewed both as possible incremental cooling mechanisms and as sensitive diagnostics of charge equilibration, deformation, and fusion dynamics in superheavy systems.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a concise scientific abstract explaining how the pre-equilibrium GDR probes the fusion path in N/Z-asymmetric and mass-asymmetric collisions.
counterfactuals.output: In heavy-ion collisions between nuclei with different neutron-to-proton ratios, fusion creates an initial displacement between the neutron and proton centers of mass. The resulting collective isovector oscillation—the pre-equilibrium giant dipole resonance (GDR), or dynamical dipole—emits prompt γ rays before statistical equilibration. Its intensity, energy spectrum, and angular anisotropy retain information on the early fusion trajectory. The γ-ray yield reflects the magnitude and damping of the entrance-channel dipole, whereas the centroid energy probes the evolving density and deformation of the composite system. Emission anisotropy constrains the dipole-axis rotation and thus the contact time and angular dynamics. In mass-asymmetric reactions, nucleon transfer, neck formation, and shape relaxation modify both the onset and lifetime of the oscillation. Consequently, systematic measurements across entrance channels leading to the same compound nucleus can isolate how N/Z and mass asymmetries govern charge equilibration, dissipation, and the transition from dinuclear configurations to a fused system.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe TDHF calculations of isovector collective excitations in fused heavy nuclei, emphasizing the effects of deformation, rotation, and vibration on the giant dipole resonance.
counterfactuals.output:
Time-dependent Hartree–Fock (TDHF) calculations describe isovector collective motion by evolving occupied single-particle orbitals self-consistently with an effective interaction, typically a Skyrme energy-density functional,

\[
i\hbar\,\frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t}=[h[\rho],\rho].
\]

For a fused heavy system, the calculation can begin either from a constrained deformed compound-nucleus state followed by a small isovector boost, or directly from a heavy-ion collision. The latter naturally includes deformation, angular momentum, shape oscillations, and pre-equilibrium dipole motion.

### Extracting the giant dipole resonance

The relevant collective coordinate is the neutron–proton center-of-mass separation,

\[
D_i(t)=\frac{NZ}{A}\left[R_{p,i}(t)-R_{n,i}(t)\right].
\]

A weak opposite boost of protons and neutrons gives the linear-response dipole strength. The Fourier transform of \(D_i(t)\), or of its second derivative for emitted radiation, yields the dipole strength or \(\gamma\)-ray spectrum. In collision calculations, a dipole can also arise without an external boost when projectile and target have different \(N/Z\); this is the dynamical or pre-equilibrium dipole mode.

### Effect of deformation

A deformed fused nucleus has different restoring forces along its principal axes. The GDR therefore splits into components polarized parallel and perpendicular to the symmetry axis:

- In a prolate system, the long-axis mode generally lies at lower energy because the restoring force is weaker over the larger dimension.
- The two transverse modes occur at higher energy and are degenerate if the shape is axially symmetric.
- Oblate or triaxial configurations produce a different ordering or three distinct components.

TDHF follows the instantaneous density, so the resonance energies change as the fused system elongates, contracts, or evolves toward a compact shape. Strong early-time deformation can shift dipole strength well below the equilibrium GDR and can generate broad or fragmented spectra when the shape changes during the oscillation.

### Rotation

Noncentral fusion produces a rotating deformed compound system. Although the intrinsic dipole frequencies are set mainly by the principal-axis lengths, the axes themselves rotate relative to the laboratory frame. Consequently, a dipole oscillation excited along one intrinsic direction is observed as a time-dependent mixture of laboratory components. This causes:

- redistribution of strength among polarization directions,
- sidebands or apparent splitting associated with the rotational frequency,
- modulation of the emitted \(\gamma\)-ray signal,
- angular anisotropy of the radiation.

For a slowly rotating nucleus, the spectrum resembles that of a static deformed shape with rotational modulation. When the rotational period becomes comparable to the dipole period, Coriolis-like coupling and changing orientation can substantially modify the line shape.

### Coupling to shape vibrations

The fused nucleus is usually not stationary: monopole, quadrupole, and sometimes octupole vibrations are excited during capture. These modes periodically alter the nuclear dimensions and hence the dipole restoring force. The GDR then behaves approximately as an oscillator with a time-dependent frequency,

\[
\ddot D(t)+\omega_D^2[Q_{20}(t),Q_{30}(t),\ldots]D(t)\simeq 0.
\]

This coupling produces frequency modulation, sidebands, fragmentation, and additional damping. Quadrupole motion is especially important because it changes the longitudinal and transverse dipole frequencies in opposite ways. Large-amplitude shape oscillations can make the distinction between a single resonance and deformation-split branches time dependent.

### Physical interpretation and limitations

TDHF captures these effects coherently and without imposing separate models for rotation, vibration, and dipole motion: all arise from the same evolving mean field. It includes one-body dissipation, Landau fragmentation, particle emission, and coupling to collective shape degrees of freedom. The predicted GDR is therefore sensitive to the entrance-channel mass and charge asymmetry, impact parameter, angular momentum, transient deformation, and the isovector part of the energy-density functional.

Standard TDHF does not fully include two-body collisional damping, thermal fluctuations, or statistical compound-nucleus decay. As a result, calculated widths may be narrower or more structured than experimental hot-GDR spectra. Nevertheless, TDHF is particularly useful for showing that the GDR in a newly fused heavy nucleus is not simply the equilibrium resonance of the final compound nucleus: it is a time-dependent response whose energy, splitting, polarization, and damping encode the simultaneous deformation, rotation, and vibration of the evolving system.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Prepare a journal-style abstract about experimental evidence for lowered pre-equilibrium GDR energies and the resulting enhancement of fusion-evaporation survival in radioactive-beam reactions.
counterfactuals.output: **Abstract—**We report experimental evidence that the giant dipole resonance (GDR) populated during the pre-equilibrium stage of radioactive-beam fusion occurs at energies below those expected for an equilibrated compound nucleus. Prompt high-energy γ-ray spectra, measured in coincidence with evaporation residues and light charged particles, reveal an excess yield at reduced γ-ray energies that cannot be reproduced using conventional equilibrium-GDR systematics. Dynamical calculations incorporating entrance-channel asymmetry, incomplete isospin equilibration, and the evolving deformation of the composite system reproduce the observed spectral shift. The lowered pre-equilibrium GDR energy increases the probability of prompt dipole emission while reducing the excitation energy available for subsequent particle evaporation. Statistical-model analyses constrained by the γ-ray data consequently predict smaller neutron-emission widths relative to fission and other loss channels during the earliest stages of de-excitation, leading to enhanced survival of fusion-evaporation residues. The measured residue yields are consistent with this cooling mechanism and exceed calculations that assume an equilibrium GDR throughout the reaction. These results establish pre-equilibrium dipole radiation as a measurable contributor to compound-nucleus survival and suggest that neutron-rich radioactive beams may provide an additional pathway for increasing evaporation-residue production in reactions aimed at accessing highly fissile and exotic nuclei.
